props.title: Turbulence

sections.content: **Turbulence** (1997) epitomizes the wave of high-altitude action thrillers that gained altitude in the 1990s, following the success of **Die Hard 2** (1990) and **Passenger 57** (1992). Ray Liotta delivers an unnervingly psychotic performance as Ryan Weaver, a serial killer who wreaks havoc on a Christmas Eve flight. Lauren Holly's flight attendant character Teri Halloran represents the era's trend of empowered female protagonists fighting back, similar to Sandra Bullock in **Speed** (1994) and Jodie Foster in **Flightplan** (2005).

sections.content: The late 1990s marked a peculiar fascination with airborne action, with 1997 particularly packed with aviation thrillers. Air Force One (1997), Con Air (1997), and **Turbulence** (1997) all premiered within months of each other, each escalating the stakes of mid-air mayhem. These films capitalized on growing air travel anxieties and pre-9/11 security concerns, while maintaining a distinctly 90s approach to action entertainment - big budgets, practical effects, and star-driven vehicles.

**Turbulence** stands out for its slasher-film elements, effectively combining the claustrophobia of airplane thrillers with horror movie tropes. This hybrid approach preceded similar genre-blending efforts like Red Eye (2005) and Non-Stop (2014). The film's Christmas setting also places it in a unique subcategory alongside **Die Hard** (1988) and **Reindeer Games** (2000) - action films that use holiday themes as an ironic backdrop for violence. sections.content: While **Airport** (1970) established the template for aviation disaster films, **Turbulence** represents the more action-oriented, villain-driven approach that dominated the 90s. This shift from disaster to action-thriller continued through films like **Snakes on a Plane** (2006) and **7500** (2019), though none matched the pure bombastic excess of the 1997 trifecta of airplane action films. The genre's evolution reflects changing audience expectations and security concerns, with modern entries like **Flightplan** (2005) and Non-Stop (2014) incorporating post-9/11 themes and technology.
